doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Getting a radio and music in the family home
summary: The radio brought Duke Ellington broadcasts; Audre relays family stories of music in his grandmother's house and riverboat dances.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Still gravel roads in the ‘50s. But in the 1930s and early ‘40s, you’re going to Charleston High School, and I gather that once you got... The radio would have arrived in 1940 or 1941—you mentioned getting one when you were 13.
That probably would have expanded your listening and access to hearing a lot of music?
Oh, I don’t know... I just remember having the radio. I used to listen to that. I used to get the Duke Ellington band... They were playing broadcasts for War Bonds.

I remember all the stories that your aunts would tell about...at your grandmother’s house... There was a lot of music in the house. They used to roll back the rugs and dance, and your mother played ukelele...
Yes. Well, you don’t remember, then.

When I was down there, I talked to all his aunts all the time about that, and they said when she first came down she would sit up on the piano and play that ukelele... They really at first didn’t like her because she took their handsome brother or something like that.
But they talked about...that was what they did for entertainment. So there must have been a lot of music.
Well, I remember my parents used to go to the riverboat, to dances. That was about 40 miles away, something...
Was that on the Mississippi River?
